rawSteps.primaryIntent: Using the official Python documentation, locate the built-in zip() function and report (1) which Python version added the 'strict' parameter and (2) what happens when strict=True and the iterables have different lengths.
rawSteps.reasoning: The agent navigated directly to the zip() anchor on the official Python documentation (the /library/functions.html#zip URL resolves to /builtins/functions.html#zip, the same page), and its extract call at step 2 returned the zip() documentation including the signature zip(*iterables, strict=False) and the note 'Changed in version 3.10: Added the strict argument.' The rendered page (screenshot) confirms the strict=True behavior: 'Unlike the default behavior, it raises a ValueError if one iterable is exhausted before the others,' with the example traceback ('ValueError: zip() argument 2 is longer than argument 1'). The agent's final answer accurately reports both facts: strict was added in Python 3.10, and strict=True raises ValueError on unequal-length iterables (vs. the default behavior of stopping at the shortest iterable). Both rubric criteria are fully satisfied with sufficient evidence; no hallucination or contradiction is present.

result.zip_docs:
zip(*iterables, strict=False)

Iterate over several iterables in parallel, producing tuples with an item from each one.

Example:

>>> for item in zip([1, 2, 3], ['sugar', 'spice', 'everything nice']):
...     print(item)
...
(1, 'sugar')
(2, 'spice')
(3, 'everything nice')

More formally: zip() returns an iterator of tuples, where the i-th tuple contains the i-th element from each of the argument iterables.

Another way to think of zip() is that it turns rows into columns, and columns into rows. This is similar to transposing a matrix.

zip() is lazy: The elements won’t be processed until the iterable is iterated on, e.g. by a for loop or by wrapping in a list.

One thing to consider is that the iterables passed to zip() could have different lengths; sometimes by design, and sometimes because of a bug in the code that prepared these iterables. Python offers three different approaches to dealing with this issue:

• By default, zip() stops when the shortest iterable is exhausted. It will ignore the remaining items in the longer iterables, cutting off the result to the length of the shortest iterable:

>>> list(zip(range(3), ['fee', 'fi', 'fo', 'fum']))
[(0, 'fee'), (1, 'fi'), (2, 'fo')]

• zip() is often used in cases where the iterables are assumed to be of equal length. In such cases, it’s recommended to use the strict=True option. Its output is the same as regular zip():

>>> list(zip(('a', 'b', 'c'), (1, 2, 3), strict=True))
[('a', 1), ('b', 2), ('c', 3)]

Unlike the default behavior, it raises a ValueError if one iterable is exhausted before the others:

>>> for item in zip(range(3), ['fee', 'fi', 'fo', 'fum'], strict=True):
...     print(item)
...
(0, 'fee')
(1, 'fi')
(2, 'fo')
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
ValueError: zip() argument 2 is longer than argument 1

Without the strict=True argument, any bug that results in iterables of different lengths will be silenced, possibly manifesting as a hard-to-find bug in another part of the program.

• Shorter iterables can be padded with a constant value to make all the iterables have the same length. This is done by itertools.zip_longest().

Edge cases: With a single iterable argument, zip() returns an iterator of 1-tuples. With no arguments, it returns an empty iterator.

Tips and tricks:

• The left-to-right evaluation order of the iterables is guaranteed. This makes possible an idiom for clustering a data series into n-length groups using zip(*[iter(s)]*n, strict=True). This repeats the same iterator n times so that each output tuple has the result of n calls to the iterator. This has the effect of dividing the input into n-length chunks.

• zip() in conjunction with the * operator can be used to unzip a list:

>>> x = [1, 2, 3]
>>> y = [4, 5, 6]
>>> list(zip(x, y))
[(1, 4), (2, 5), (3, 6)]
>>> x2, y2 = zip(*zip(x, y))
>>> x == list(x2) and y == list(y2)
True

Changed in version 3.10: Added the strict argument.

input.instruction: Extract the full documentation text for the built-in zip() function, including its signature, description of the strict parameter, and all "Changed in version" / "Added in version" notes.

result.version_notes: Changed in version 3.10: Added the strict argument.
result.zip_docs:
zip(*iterables, strict=False)

Iterate over several iterables in parallel, producing tuples with an item from each one.

Example:

>>> for item in zip([1, 2, 3], ['sugar', 'spice', 'everything nice']):
...     print(item)
...
(1, 'sugar')
(2, 'spice')
(3, 'everything nice')

More formally: zip() returns an iterator of tuples, where the i-th tuple contains the i-th element from each of the argument iterables.

Another way to think of zip() is that it turns rows into columns, and columns into rows. This is similar to transposing a matrix.

zip() is lazy: The elements won’t be processed until the iterable is iterated on, e.g. by a for loop or by wrapping in a list.

One thing to consider is that the iterables passed to zip() could have different lengths; sometimes by design, and sometimes because of a bug in the code that prepared these iterables. Python offers three different approaches to dealing with this issue:

• By default, zip() stops when the shortest iterable is exhausted. It will ignore the remaining items in the longer iterables, cutting off the result to the length of the shortest iterable:

>>> list(zip(range(3), ['fee', 'fi', 'fo', 'fum']))
[(0, 'fee'), (1, 'fi'), (2, 'fo')]

• zip() is often used in cases where the iterables are assumed to be of equal length. In such cases, it’s recommended to use the strict=True option. Its output is the same as regular zip():

>>> list(zip(('a', 'b', 'c'), (1, 2, 3), strict=True))
[('a', 1), ('b', 2), ('c', 3)]

Unlike the default behavior, it raises a ValueError if one iterable is exhausted before the others:

>>> for item in zip(range(3), ['fee', 'fi', 'fo', 'fum'], strict=True):
...     print(item)
...
(0, 'fee')
(1, 'fi')
(2, 'fo')
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
ValueError: zip() argument 2 is longer than argument 1

Without the strict=True argument, any bug that results in iterables of different lengths will be silenced, possibly manifesting as a hard-to-find bug in another part of the program.

• Shorter iterables can be padded with a constant value to make all the iterables have the same length. This is done by itertools.zip_longest().

Edge cases: With a single iterable argument, zip() returns an iterator of 1-tuples. With no arguments, it returns an empty iterator.

Tips and tricks:

• The left-to-right evaluation order of the iterables is guaranteed. This makes possible an idiom for clustering a data series into n-length groups using zip(*[iter(s)]*n, strict=True). This repeats the same iterator n times so that each output tuple has the result of n calls to the iterator. This has the effect of dividing the input into n-length chunks.

• zip() in conjunction with the * operator can be used to unzip a list:

>>> x = [1, 2, 3]
>>> y = [4, 5, 6]
>>> list(zip(x, y))
[(1, 4), (2, 5), (3, 6)]
>>> x2, y2 = zip(*zip(x, y))
>>> x == list(x2) and y == list(y2)
True

Changed in version 3.10: Added the strict argument.

Found both required answers: (1) The 'strict' parameter was added in Python 3.10, per the doc note "Changed in version 3.10: Added the strict argument," with the signature zip(*iterables, strict=False). (2) When strict=True and one iterable is exhausted before the others, a ValueError is raised (e.g., "ValueError: zip() argument 2 is longer than argument 1"), unlike the default strict=False behavior which silently stops at the shortest iterable.
